questions.topic: Foreign-school pharmacist reciprocity: required FPGEC and internship
questions.stem: A pharmacist graduated from a non-approved foreign pharmacy school and subsequently became licensed by examination in a recognized U.S. state. The applicant is currently in good standing there, has NABP preliminary transfer approval and seeks Massachusetts pharmacist licensure by reciprocity. What must still be satisfied? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Provide the official FPGEC Certificate required by the non-approved-college reciprocity pathway.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 3.02(3)(a)1 requires official FPGEC certification.

choices.text: Skip all internship documentation solely because the applicant already holds another U.S. pharmacist license.
choices.why: Incorrect. 3.02(3)(a)2 separately requires documented qualifying internship experience.

choices.text: Earn a passing Massachusetts MPJE result and satisfy the Board's final licensure process.
choices.why: Correct. 3.02(3)(a)3 and 3.02(1)(b) preserve MPJE and Board authority.

choices.text: Begin independent Massachusetts practice immediately after NABP preliminary approval without a Board license.
choices.why: Incorrect. NABP conducts a preliminary evaluation; the Board decides final Massachusetts eligibility.

choices.text: Substitute an overseas pharmacy diploma for FPGEC certification without any Board-approved exception.
choices.why: Incorrect. 3.02(3)(a) expressly sets out FPGEC evidence for non-approved-school graduates.

questions.material_novelty: Targets extra documentation on an already-licensed foreign-graduate reciprocity application, not initial FPGEE-intern authorization or preliminary NABP approval.
questions.counterfactual_flip: For graduates of ACPE-accredited schools, the special FPGEC requirement of 3.02(3) does not apply.
questions.legal_decision: Apply foreign-graduate special reciprocity FPGEC and internship criteria.

questions.topic: Summary cease-and-desist and quarantine versus suspension hearing deadline
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives a pre-hearing emergency cease-and-desist and quarantine notice from the Board President after inspectors find a serious product safety hazard. The pharmacy owner argues that this is automatically a final disciplinary revocation and requests the seven-day suspension hearing described in 247 CMR 10.07. Under 247 CMR 10.08, which conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The notice automatically revokes the pharmacy license as a final disciplinary sanction.
choices.why: Incorrect. 10.08 provides non-disciplinary emergency restrictions pending further proceedings.

choices.text: The Board or its President may prohibit use of hazardous stock and restrict operations immediately.
choices.why: Correct. 10.08(1) authorizes emergency cease-and-desist and quarantine notices.

choices.text: The seven-day hearing provision for summary license suspension necessarily applies to this 10.08 notice.
choices.why: Incorrect. 10.08(3) specifies a separate hearing deadline for these notices.

choices.text: A limited hearing on the necessity of this notice must be afforded within 15 business days.
choices.why: Correct. The 10.08(3) hearing clock is 15 business days after the Board action.

choices.text: The restrictions continue until rescinded/amended or until final action on a related complaint.
choices.why: Correct. The notice's duration is governed by 10.08(2).

questions.material_novelty: Old E30-101 tests emergency suspension's seven-day hearing; new case concerns a different non-disciplinary cease/quarantine notice with a 15-business-day hearing.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A summary license suspension actually imposed under 10.07 would follow the seven-day necessity-hearing rule.
questions.legal_decision: Differentiate emergency operations notices from disciplinary license suspension.

questions.critical_exception: The Board issued 10.08 notices, not a 10.07 summary suspension.

questions.topic: Unlicensed vendor entering prescription area versus handling unbagged stock
questions.stem: An outside inventory vendor has no Massachusetts pharmacy personnel license. The pharmacist proposes to escort the vendor into the secured prescription area, where the vendor wants to count stock by handling unfilled prescription-drug bottles. A cashier outside the secured area wants to hand over completed pharmacist-verified bagged prescriptions. What is permitted under Board Policy 2020-15 (revised November 6, 2025)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The unlicensed vendor may enter the secured prescription area alone if a business contract is on file.
choices.why: Incorrect. An external vendor may enter only if accompanied and monitored by a pharmacist.

choices.text: The vendor may enter for appropriate work when a pharmacist accompanies and monitors the visit.
choices.why: Correct. The Board policy expressly allows monitored access by outside vendors.

choices.text: The vendor may directly handle unfilled prescription-drug inventory whenever a pharmacist watches.
choices.why: Incorrect. Anyone handling prescription medications that have not been completed, verified, and bagged must be licensed.

choices.text: An unlicensed cashier may independently counsel on prescriptions and resolve DUR alerts.
choices.why: Incorrect. Cashier authority is limited to nonclinical verified-bagged prescription sales and an offer to counsel.

choices.text: The cashier may sell already verified, bagged prescriptions and convey the pharmacist's offer to counsel.
choices.why: Correct. These are permitted limited cashier activities under the policy.

questions.material_novelty: E30-246 tested the cashier's limited role; the legal outcome here depends on separate escorted physical access and prohibited drug-stock handling by a visitor.
questions.counterfactual_flip: With a proper pharmacy staff license, the inventory worker may instead qualify to handle stock within the credential's permitted duties.
questions.legal_decision: Separate supervised physical access from professional handling of prescription drugs.

questions.critical_exception: Vendor remains unlicensed; bottles are unfinished stock, not finished bagged prescriptions.

questions.topic: CDTM mandatory supervision-gap and urgent communication agreement clauses
questions.stem: A Massachusetts community CDTM pharmacist and supervising physician have a signed hypertension agreement plus an individual patient's referral and written consent. The agreement states the disease, routine medication protocols and prescribing authority, but omits urgent-results communication, a supervision contingency when either participant is absent, and which duties can be delegated. Which revisions are legally required? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Add explicit urgent communication procedures and timing for conveying relevant test results or prescription changes.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 16.04(2)(h) mandates timing and urgent communication procedures.

choices.text: Leave the arrangements for supervising physician absence entirely to unwritten custom.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 16.04(2)(h) requires an agreement procedure when either party is absent.

choices.text: Specify the nature of supervision and how the parties handle an unavailable pharmacist or physician.
choices.why: Correct. Absence and supervision arrangements must appear in the written agreement.

choices.text: Identify which CDTM duties may or may not be delegated and the scope and duration of delegation.
choices.why: Correct. Section 16.04(3) requires explicit delegation boundaries.

choices.text: Authorize a cashier to do a pharmacist's final prescription validation if delegated in the agreement.
choices.why: Incorrect. A CDTM agreement cannot bypass the pharmacy-personnel scope restrictions in 247 CMR 8.

questions.material_novelty: Tests absent mandatory CDTM agreement clauses governing urgent communications and staff delegation rather than prescriptive scope or the 24-hour physician notification itself.
questions.counterfactual_flip: With all required communication, absence, and delegation provisions expressly written, these particular agreement deficiencies are resolved.
questions.legal_decision: Identify required agreement controls for CDTM clinical communication and delegation.

questions.critical_exception: Patient referral, consent and pharmacist qualifications already satisfied.

questions.topic: Qualified nuclear pharmacist: Board recognition and on-premises presence
questions.stem: A registered Massachusetts pharmacist with only ordinary retail experience plans to manage a nuclear pharmacy alone. The pharmacist has not been recognized by the Board as a qualified nuclear pharmacist and would consult an off-site nuclear specialist by telephone. What is the appropriate staffing decision?

choices.text: A routine Massachusetts pharmacist license alone satisfies all specialized nuclear pharmacist qualification requirements.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 13.02 requires specialized evidence and Board recognition.

choices.text: A licensed technician may manage nuclear pharmacy radiopharmaceutical activities without a qualified nuclear pharmacist present.
choices.why: Incorrect. 13.05(2)–(3) restricts management and professional activity to qualified nuclear pharmacists.

choices.text: The nuclear pharmacist needs only monthly in-person visits if telephone advice is available.
choices.why: Incorrect. 13.05(16) requires a qualified nuclear pharmacist on premises whenever the nuclear pharmacy is open.

choices.text: Have a Board-recognized qualified nuclear pharmacist personally present throughout operating hours.
choices.why: Correct. Sections 13.02 and 13.05(2)–(3),(16) require nuclear-specific qualification and on-site coverage.

choices.text: The qualification may be obtained by merely displaying a national technician certificate at the nuclear pharmacy.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Board's specialized pharmacist qualification is not a technician credential.

questions.material_novelty: No old A–E item tests nuclear-specific pharmacist recognition or required qualified on-premises coverage, unlike general retail/institutional pharmacist presence.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If this pharmacist later meets the specialized criteria and obtains Board recognition, the specific qualification defect would change.
questions.legal_decision: Distinguish qualified nuclear pharmacist from general retail pharmacist and require on-site nuclear coverage.

questions.topic: Klonopin clonazepam versus BuSpar buspirone schedules
questions.stem: A pharmacist identifies schedules for Klonopin (clonazepam) tablets and BuSpar (buspirone) tablets dispensed on otherwise valid Massachusetts prescriptions. Which federal and corresponding Massachusetts schedules are correct?

choices.text: Both Klonopin and BuSpar are Schedule IV because they are prescribed for anxiety symptoms, even though only one is a benzodiazepine.
choices.why: Incorrect. Buspirone is not federally scheduled, despite use for anxiety.

choices.text: Clonazepam is Schedule IV; buspirone is federally unscheduled and Massachusetts Schedule VI.
choices.why: Correct. Clonazepam appears in 21 CFR 1308.14(c)(13); buspirone is not a federal controlled drug.

choices.text: Clonazepam is Schedule II, and buspirone is Schedule III.
choices.why: Incorrect. Neither designation is consistent with federal scheduling.

choices.text: Both are Schedule VI because they are ordinary oral outpatient medicines.
choices.why: Incorrect. Clonazepam is federally and Massachusetts Schedule IV.

choices.text: Clonazepam is Schedule V, and buspirone is Schedule IV.
choices.why: Incorrect. The federal schedules in this choice do not match the drugs.

questions.material_novelty: Introduces an anxiolytic controlled benzodiazepine and a federally unscheduled anxiolytic not previously tested as this brand/generic/schedule decision.
questions.counterfactual_flip: For buspirone alone, federal CIII–V refill restrictions are not triggered.
questions.legal_decision: Recognize Klonopin CIV versus BuSpar non-DEA-controlled Schedule VI.

questions.topic: Talwin pentazocine versus Nubain nalbuphine scheduling
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives prescriptions for Talwin (pentazocine) and Nubain (nalbuphine) as ordinary prescription formulations. Which statement best identifies their federal and corresponding Massachusetts schedules?

choices.text: Both medicines are Schedule II because any opioid effect always requires Schedule II status.
choices.why: Incorrect. Federal scheduling gives pentazocine Schedule IV and specifically excludes nalbuphine from the opium/opiate category.

choices.text: Talwin is Schedule III, while Nubain is Schedule V.
choices.why: Incorrect. Neither classification appears in the cited federal schedule entries.

choices.text: Both are federally uncontrolled drugs and Massachusetts Schedule VI.
choices.why: Incorrect. Pentazocine is explicitly listed in federal Schedule IV.

choices.text: Talwin is Schedule V and Nubain Schedule III because one is an injectable medicine.
choices.why: Incorrect. Dosage form does not make these stated schedule assignments.

choices.text: Talwin is Schedule IV; Nubain is federally unscheduled and Massachusetts Schedule VI.
choices.why: Correct. Pentazocine is under 1308.14(g)(1), while nalbuphine is specifically excluded from 1308.12(b)(1).

questions.material_novelty: A new pairing of structurally related analgesics whose federal scheduling differs despite opioid action, distinct from Nucynta/Ultram or codeine formulation cases.
questions.counterfactual_flip: Replacing pentazocine with nalbuphine changes which drug is federally controlled.
questions.legal_decision: Differentiate pentazocine CIV versus nalbuphine federally unscheduled.

questions.topic: Pharmacist DoxyPEP: prevention, exposure window and protocol
questions.stem: A qualified Massachusetts pharmacist has completed the required accredited STI-prevention training and evaluates an adult who has already been found eligible under the current Massachusetts DoxyPEP statewide guidance. The patient asks to take 200 mg doxycycline 48 hours after a qualifying exposure and then take a second 200 mg dose 12 hours later. No other contraindication exists. Which are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The first 200-mg dose is within the generally recommended 72-hour postexposure window.
choices.why: Correct. Massachusetts DoxyPEP guidance describes 200 mg as soon as possible, no later than 72 hours after exposure.

choices.text: The pharmacist must prescribe repeated 200-mg doses every 12 hours for all patients regardless of exposure.
choices.why: Incorrect. DoxyPEP is an exposure-linked preventive intervention and not an automatic 400-mg/day course.

choices.text: The proposed additional 200 mg in the same 24-hour period exceeds the guidance's 200-mg daily maximum.
choices.why: Correct. The state patient guidance states not to take more than 200 mg in any 24 hours.

choices.text: DoxyPEP is a substitute for HIV PrEP or PEP because doxycycline prevents viral HIV infection.
choices.why: Incorrect. The state explicitly distinguishes bacterial STI prevention from HIV prevention.

choices.text: A properly qualified pharmacist may use the §19F pharmacist-prescribing pathway if all statewide eligibility and documentation requirements are met.
choices.why: Correct. DCP 26-08-125 and its current DoxyPEP guidance include this pharmacist prescribing pathway.

questions.citation: M.G.L. c.94C §19F; DPH Circular DCP 26-08-125; DPH DoxyPEP statewide guidance (2026)
questions.material_novelty: E071 focuses which training is required for STI prevention versus treatment; this directly tests DoxyPEP postexposure timing, dose repetition and prevention-versus-HIV distinctions.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A second 200-mg dose at least 24 hours later after a separate qualifying exposure would be evaluated differently under the prevention protocol.
questions.legal_decision: Apply DoxyPEP timing, daily maximum and separate HIV/STI prevention indication.

questions.topic: 2026 DEA anesthesia drug: cipepofol versus propofol
questions.stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy reviews injectable cipepofol and Diprivan (propofol), both used as anesthetic/sedative drugs. The dispensing protocol relies on the federal drug schedules in effect November 2026. Which classification is correct?

choices.text: Both agents are federal Schedule II because they are administered intravenously.
choices.why: Incorrect. IV administration is not by itself a criterion for Schedule II scheduling.

choices.text: Cipepofol is federally uncontrolled because it is a close analogue of propofol.
choices.why: Incorrect. DEA formally scheduled cipepofol in Schedule IV in August 2026.

choices.text: Cipepofol is federal Schedule IV; propofol remains federally unscheduled and ordinarily Massachusetts Schedule VI.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1308.14(c)(11) includes cipepofol, while the DEA's 2026 propofol document identifies it as not CSA-scheduled.

choices.text: Propofol is Schedule II and cipepofol is Schedule I.
choices.why: Incorrect. Neither designation matches current federal scheduling.

choices.text: Both are Schedule V because the drugs are used by anesthesia specialists.
choices.why: Incorrect. Scheduling is drug-specific; specialty or setting does not dictate the schedule.

questions.citation: 21 CFR 1308.14(c)(11); DEA Cipepofol interim final rule 91 FR 55259 (effective 08/27/2026); DEA Propofol Drug & Chemical of Concern (04/2026)
questions.material_novelty: Tests 2026 newly controlled anesthetic cipepofol versus the older unscheduled propofol, unlike pentobarbital/phenobarbital or zuranolone.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If cipepofol had not yet reached its federal final-rule effective date, the scheduling decision would need that prior legal snapshot.
questions.legal_decision: Identify 2026 cipepofol CIV and federally unscheduled propofol.

questions.topic: 2026 pharmacist administration: long-acting injectable and OTP exception
questions.stem: A qualified Massachusetts retail pharmacist has required medication-administration training, current CPR and valid patient-specific prescriptions for single-dose intramuscular products. One adult needs long-acting injectable aripiprazole for mental illness; another needs single-dose injectable naltrexone for substance-use disorder. A third request is for outpatient methadone administration for OUD at this retail site, which is not a registered opioid treatment program. Which conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The pharmacist may administer the eligible single-dose aripiprazole injection if all current circular requirements are satisfied.
choices.why: Correct. DCP 26-03-124 lists long-acting injectable aripiprazole as eligible for pharmacist or intern administration.

choices.text: The eligible injectable naltrexone administration may occur under the circular without an independent pharmacist MCSR solely for dispensing by administration.
choices.why: Correct. The circular lists naltrexone and provides a specific no-separate-MCSR administration pathway when all conditions are satisfied.

choices.text: The retail pharmacy may administer methadone for OUD on the same basis as an authorized outpatient injectable.
choices.why: Incorrect. The circular limits administering methadone for addiction treatment to a registered opioid treatment program.

choices.text: The administration pathway requires a valid prescription; it does not automatically authorize the pharmacist to originate every requested prescription.
choices.why: Correct. The circular's authorized dispensing-by-administration route is separate from any specific pharmacist-prescribing power.

choices.text: A pharmacy technician may independently administer the listed drug merely because the pharmacist holds CPR certification.
choices.why: Incorrect. The circular authorizes appropriately qualified pharmacists and pharmacy interns; other role-specific authorities must be separately established.

questions.material_novelty: Adds 2026 DPH administration of LAI antipsychotic and naltrexone versus methadone OUD at non-OTP retail, not previous HIV prevention injection or testosterone scope.
questions.counterfactual_flip: At a properly registered OTP with an appropriate order, methadone administration has a separately authorized pathway.
questions.legal_decision: Separate pharmacist administration permissions for eligible LAIs from methadone OTP limitation.

questions.topic: First opioid prescription: OUD-treatment exception to Massachusetts seven-day limit
questions.stem: A Massachusetts physician issues an otherwise valid initial 28-day Schedule III buprenorphine/naloxone prescription specifically for treatment of opioid use disorder in an adult outpatient. The patient has never received an opioid prescription before. The pharmacist asks whether the seven-day first-opioid limit in M.G.L. c.94C §19D necessarily restricts this OUD treatment to seven days. Which answer is correct?

choices.text: No. The statute expressly exempts opioids prescribed for treatment of substance use disorder.
choices.why: Correct. M.G.L. c.94C §19D(c) exempts prescriptions issued for treatment of substance use disorder from the seven-day restriction in subsection (a).

choices.text: Yes. Every first opioid prescription is subject to seven days, even when prescribed for OUD treatment.
choices.why: Incorrect. The special SUD treatment exclusion is expressly in §19D(c).

choices.text: Yes, unless the patient first receives a separate Schedule II opioid prescription for analgesia.
choices.why: Incorrect. A prior analgesic prescription is not the prerequisite for the SUD-treatment exemption.

choices.text: No, because buprenorphine is not a controlled substance under federal law.
choices.why: Incorrect. Buprenorphine is federally Schedule III; its drug-scheduling status does not create this exemption.

choices.text: No, because Massachusetts never imposes a seven-day prescribing limit on any initial opioid prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 19D(a) generally imposes a seven-day limit on qualifying initial opioid prescriptions, subject to specific exceptions.

questions.material_novelty: Instead of a general 7-day pain-opioid limit, this tests the specifically carved-out initial Schedule III buprenorphine/naloxone treatment of OUD.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the opioid is instead issued for an adult's first routine acute-pain treatment without a qualifying exception, the ordinary seven-day rule must be considered.
questions.legal_decision: Recognize the substance-use-disorder treatment exclusion from the first opioid prescription duration cap.

questions.topic: Federal conditional nonprescription Schedule V dispensing limits and professional responsibility
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is reviewing the federal rule for a hypothetical Schedule V preparation that is lawfully approved for nonprescription sale, is NOT required by federal law to bear the Rx-only legend, and independently meets all Massachusetts conditions for nonprescription dispensing. The proposal is to let a 17-year-old buy it from a cashier without pharmacist involvement or recording. Which federal rules apply? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: A pharmacist must personally dispense a Schedule V substance supplied without a prescription under the specified federal pathway.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1306.26(a) permits only a pharmacist to conduct the professional nonprescription sale under this limited rule.

choices.text: Any retail cashier can independently make the Schedule V nonprescription sale whenever the product is behind the counter.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 1306.26(a) prohibits a nonpharmacist from making the professional dispensing decision, even under pharmacist supervision; a nonpharmacist may perform only the permitted cash/delivery step afterward.

choices.text: The buyer may be under 18 when a parent sends them, and federal §1306.26 contains no minimum age.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 1306.26(c) prohibits dispensing to a person younger than 18 years.

choices.text: The pharmacist must maintain the federally required purchaser and dispensing record for the nonprescription transaction.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1306.26(e) specifies the special written record with purchaser identity, product, amount, date, and pharmacist information.

choices.text: The federal allowance does not override a state law or FDA prescription-only restriction that would otherwise prohibit an OTC sale.
choices.why: Correct. The introductory FDA prescription-only condition and 21 CFR 1306.26(f) require that no other federal, state, or local law demand a prescription.

questions.citation: 21 CFR 1306.26 introductory paragraph, (a),(c)–(g), including state-law preservation
questions.material_novelty: Uses an explicitly hypothetical legally nonprescription Schedule V preparation to test the federal pharmacist-only, 18-year-old and recordkeeping conditions, without incorrectly claiming Rx-only cough products can be sold OTC in Massachusetts.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the product is prescription-only federally or in Massachusetts, the §1306.26 nonprescription pathway cannot be used even by a pharmacist.
questions.legal_decision: Identify federal conditions on legally permissible nonprescription dispensing of certain Schedule V products.

questions.topic: Schedule II opioid dispensing: risk information and antagonist offer
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is preparing a legitimate Schedule II opioid prescription for an adult patient. The pharmacist has completed clinical review and ordinary counseling. A technician suggests that the pharmacy need not discuss overdose risk or offer access to an opioid antagonist because the patient already has a prescription. Which additional conclusions follow from M.G.L. c.94C §18D? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The statutory pharmacist duties apply only if the opioid is Schedule IV or Schedule V.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 18D(b) specifically addresses a pharmacist dispensing Schedule II opioid prescriptions.

choices.text: The pharmacist must inform the patient of potential adverse risks of the Schedule II opioid.
choices.why: Correct. M.G.L. c.94C §18D(b) expressly requires information about the potential adverse risks of a Schedule II opioid.

choices.text: The pharmacist must require the patient to purchase an opioid antagonist as a condition of every Schedule II opioid dispensing.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 18D(b) requires offering the antagonist; it does not make purchase or acceptance mandatory.

choices.text: The pharmacist must offer to dispense an opioid antagonist in accordance with the statute and applicable standing-order authority.
choices.why: Correct. The antagonist offer is a separate statutory pharmacist duty.

choices.text: A technician's confirmation that the prescription is electronically signed eliminates all statutory counseling or antagonist obligations.
choices.why: Incorrect. Electronic authenticity does not waive the information and offer duties in §18D(b).

questions.citation: M.G.L. c.94C §18D(a) (definition of opioid antagonist), (b) (pharmacist risk information and offer)
questions.material_novelty: Unlike Schedule II/III printed consumer educational pamphlets and naloxone sales, this question isolates the pharmacist's Schedule II opioid risk-discussion and antagonist offer duties.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A Schedule VI nonopioid prescription does not trigger this particular §18D(b) opioid-specific rule.
questions.legal_decision: Distinguish pharmacist obligation to offer an antagonist from mandatory sale or prescriber obligations.

questions.topic: 2026 reproductive and gender-affirming prescription label shielding: Schedule VI only
questions.stem: A Massachusetts prescriber sends a NEW Schedule VI estradiol prescription for a patient's gender-affirming care, expressly asks the pharmacist to use the prescriber's health care practice name instead of the individual prescriber's name on the patient-facing pharmacy container label, and supplies both names in the underlying signed prescription. The pharmacy also has an unrelated federal Schedule III testosterone prescription. Which statements accurately apply the Massachusetts rule effective January 1, 2026? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: For the qualifying Schedule VI prescription, the pharmacist must use the requested practice name instead of the individual prescriber's name on the container label.
choices.why: Correct. Chapter 16 of Acts of 2025, §7, effective January 1, 2026, and the Board advisory create this prescriber-requested Schedule VI labeling provision.

choices.text: The pharmacy must delete the individual prescriber's identity from the underlying prescription and audit records.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Board advisory requires retaining prescriber identity in the underlying prescription record.

choices.text: The pharmacist should retain the prescriber's identity in records even though the qualifying patient-facing label shows the practice name.
choices.why: Correct. The label substitution does not waive recordkeeping and practitioner identification requirements.

choices.text: The same Massachusetts rule automatically removes the individual prescriber's name from all federally controlled Schedule III testosterone labels regardless of federal law.
choices.why: Incorrect. The 2025 amendment is subject to federal law, and the December 2025 Massachusetts Board guidance expressly describes the practice-name labeling pathway for Schedule VI medicines, not federal Schedule III testosterone.

choices.text: The request and alternative labeling apply to authorized refills of that qualifying new Schedule VI prescription, as directed by the Board guidance.
choices.why: Correct. The December 2025 Board advisory describes how the documented request carries over to refills.

questions.citation: Acts 2025, c.16, §7 (effective 2026-01-01), amending M.G.L. c.94C §21; Massachusetts Board Advisory: Prescription Labeling for Reproductive and Gender-Affirming Medications (2025)
questions.material_novelty: This tests a new prescriber-requested, privacy-protective patient-facing label for Schedule VI reproductive/gender-affirming treatment, not general prescriber identification or controlled-testosterone administration.
questions.counterfactual_flip: Without a prescriber's specific request on the qualifying new Schedule VI prescription, the ordinary prescriber-name labeling standard applies.
questions.legal_decision: Apply the January 2026 shielding law to prescription container label but not dispensing records or federally scheduled drugs.

questions.topic: Prescriber personally dispensing controlled medication: MGL §22 label rather than pharmacist label
questions.stem: A Massachusetts-authorized practitioner lawfully dispenses a small Schedule VI outpatient medication supply directly from the practitioner's own office to a human patient, rather than sending the prescription to a community pharmacy. It is not an immediate administration of a dose during a visit. The practitioner proposes a vial marked only 'take as directed.' What must happen?

choices.text: The practitioner can omit labeling because only pharmacies are responsible for prescription container labels.
choices.why: Incorrect. M.G.L. c.94C §22(b) imposes labeling obligations on registered practitioners who directly dispense controlled substances.

choices.text: The patient may self-select any handwritten label at home, because the practitioner did not send the prescription to a pharmacy.
choices.why: Incorrect. A patient's later home label does not discharge the practitioner's statutory dispensing-label duty.

choices.text: The practitioner must affix the identification, drug, dosage and directions required for a direct dispensing under §22(b).
choices.why: Correct. Section 22(b) specifies the practitioner/patient identity, dispensing date, medication identity, dose, directions and cautions for direct dispensing.

choices.text: The practitioner may use an unlabeled vial whenever the amount supplied is fewer than ten tablets.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 22(b) does not make a blanket exemption for small quantities.

choices.text: Only DEA Schedule II drugs require this direct-dispensing labeling; Schedule VI is excluded from M.G.L. c.94C.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 22(b) covers the controlled substance distributed under Massachusetts law, including Schedule VI.

questions.material_novelty: Moves from a pharmacy's ordinary §21 container labeling to a registered practitioner's own §22(b) patient dispensing obligations.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the practitioner directly administers a dose at the visit rather than dispensing stock to patient for later use, the direct-to-patient labeling facts would change.
questions.legal_decision: Recognize professional and container-label duties for lawful practitioner direct dispensing.

questions.topic: Long-acting non-abuse-deterrent opioid: prescriber assessment and pain-management agreement
questions.stem: A Massachusetts practitioner is considering a FIRST outpatient prescription for a long-acting, extended-release opioid that is not formulated to be abuse-deterrent. It is intended for chronic long-term pain treatment. The practitioner has not documented clinical appropriateness or discussed abuse risk, and has not signed a written pain-management treatment agreement with the patient. Which steps are required under M.G.L. c.94C §18A before proceeding? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Evaluate the underlying medical condition, substance-use risk, medication history and whether the proposed opioid is appropriate.
choices.why: Correct. Section 18A(a) requires a clinical assessment before first prescribing this non-abuse-deterrent long-acting opioid.

choices.text: Skip a treatment agreement because it is required only for Schedule VI medicines.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 18A(b) requires a written agreement for patients prescribed opioids for long-term pain management.

choices.text: Inform the patient and document why the prescriber considers the proposed opioid an appropriate course of treatment.
choices.why: Correct. Section 18A(a)(ii) requires informing the patient and documenting the clinical judgment that the drug is appropriate based on medical need.

choices.text: Use a Schedule III prescription without physician consultation solely to avoid the special opioid obligations.
choices.why: Incorrect. Changing labels or ignoring treatment risks cannot waive §18A's substance and clinical conditions.

choices.text: Maintain a written treatment agreement addressing the relevant risks, responsibilities and treatment expectations for long-term pain.
choices.why: Correct. Section 18A(b) requires a written agreement for a patient placed on long-term opioid pain management.

questions.material_novelty: Examines pre-prescribing risk assessment for first long-acting, non-abuse-deterrent opioid and a written chronic-pain treatment agreement, not a technician's handling restriction or initial opioid 7-day cap.
questions.counterfactual_flip: An initial medication for a separate acute condition not planned as long-term pain management would not automatically trigger the same §18A(b) agreement.
questions.legal_decision: Apply first long-acting non-abuse-deterrent opioid clinical evaluation and patient information/documentation, with written agreement for chronic pain.

questions.topic: Facility pharmacy licensing cycles: ordinary drug store versus sterile and complex nonsterile
questions.stem: A licensed Massachusetts business operates an ordinary Drug Store Pharmacy and maintains separate required facility licenses for sterile compounding and complex nonsterile compounding. Administration proposes treating all three licenses as a single biennial registration expiring in even-numbered years. Which statements are correct under 247 CMR 6.05–6.07? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The ordinary Drug Store Pharmacy license is renewed biennially and expires December 31 of an odd-numbered year.
choices.why: Correct. Section 6.05(2) sets the ordinary Drug Store Pharmacy's two-year cycle and December 31 odd-year expiration.

choices.text: Every specialty compounding facility license follows exactly the same odd-year expiration cycle as the ordinary Drug Store Pharmacy license.
choices.why: Incorrect. Sections 6.06(3)(a) and 6.07(3)(a) prescribe annual specialty-license expirations.

choices.text: The Sterile Compounding Pharmacy license has an annual December 31 expiration.
choices.why: Correct. Section 6.06(3)(a) expressly sets yearly expiration.

choices.text: The Complex Non-Sterile Compounding Pharmacy license also has an annual December 31 expiration.
choices.why: Correct. Section 6.07(3)(a) sets the same annual expiration for that separate facility license.

choices.text: A current pharmacist personal license automatically replaces all facility licenses for specialty compounding.
choices.why: Incorrect. Individual pharmacist licensure does not substitute for the different facility licenses in 6.05–6.07.

questions.material_novelty: Tests three *facility license* renewal cycles under 247 CMR 6, distinct from MCSR registration cycles and nonresident specialty endorsements.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a site holds only a conventional drug-store license and no specialty licenses, the additional annual specialty cycles do not arise.
questions.legal_decision: Distinguish biennial retail pharmacy facility license from separate annual sterile/complex nonsterile licenses.

questions.topic: New pharmacy must open within one year after application approval
questions.stem: A Massachusetts applicant receives Board approval of its ordinary Drug Store Pharmacy license application but leaves the site unopened for fourteen months due to construction delays. The Board has not given written permission for a later opening date. Which action is most consistent with 247 CMR 6.04(7)?

choices.text: The pharmacy can commence operating whenever construction ends; approval never has a time limit.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 6.04(7) imposes a one-calendar-year opening deadline after Board application approval.

choices.text: The site may dispense before the Board's required licensure conditions are met if the owner signs a delayed-opening declaration.
choices.why: Incorrect. A delayed opening does not itself authorize dispensing before licensing and operational requirements are satisfied.

choices.text: A pharmacist's individual professional license automatically extends the pharmacy's opening deadline indefinitely.
choices.why: Incorrect. The facility deadline is not extended by an individual's personal registration.

choices.text: Obtain the Board's written approval to extend the opening date; ordinary approval alone did not permit a fourteen-month delay.
choices.why: Correct. Section 6.04(7) requires opening within one year unless the Board provides written permission for an alternative timeframe.

choices.text: A new building permit always replaces the pharmacy Board approval and eliminates the separate opening deadline.
choices.why: Incorrect. Local construction permission does not displace 247 CMR 6.04(7).

questions.material_novelty: Unlike the separate one-year nonresident provisional-license cap in E078, this tests the one-year after approval deadline to *open* an ordinary new Massachusetts pharmacy.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the Board expressly issues written permission for later opening, the specific 14-month delay can be authorized.
questions.legal_decision: Distinguish pre-opening facility application approval from an indefinite permission not to open.

questions.topic: Specialty pharmacy licensure requires satisfactory pre-issuance inspection
questions.stem: A company applies for a Massachusetts Drug Store Pharmacy license and, for the same facility, wants licenses to prepare sterile compounds and complex nonsterile compounds. It has submitted the required plans but has not passed any Board inspection for these specialty services. Which statements follow from 247 CMR 6.04, 6.06 and 6.07? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: A Sterile Compounding Pharmacy license requires a satisfactory Board inspection before that specialty license is issued.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 6.06(2)(b) specifies a satisfactory Board inspection before specialty licensure.

choices.text: A complete written application alone automatically authorizes immediate sterile compounding before any Board inspection.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Board's satisfactory specialty inspection is a pre-issuance requirement.

choices.text: All ordinary Drug Store Pharmacy applications must undergo the identical specialized sterile-facility inspection.
choices.why: Incorrect. The ordinary initial application rule has different Board inspection discretion and cannot be treated as a sterile-qualification mandate.

choices.text: A Complex Non-Sterile Compounding Pharmacy license likewise requires a satisfactory Board inspection before issuance.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 6.07(2)(b) provides a parallel pre-issuance specialty requirement.

choices.text: The facility may manufacture and dispense compounded sterile and complex nonsterile products using only an individual pharmacist license.
choices.why: Incorrect. Massachusetts requires the applicable facility licenses and inspections; an individual pharmacist credential is not a facility license.

questions.material_novelty: Tests specialty pre-licensure inspection specifically and distinguishes it from discretionary ordinary drug-store inspection, rather than prior post-approval remodeling or 503B FDA inspection.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A facility that completed satisfactory specialty inspection and obtained the licenses can lawfully provide those specialty services if all other requirements are met.
questions.legal_decision: Distinguish special mandatory prelicense site inspection for sterile and complex nonsterile from ordinary Drug Store facility process.

questions.topic: Facility renewal attestation of all mandatory 247 CMR 20 reporting
questions.stem: A Massachusetts licensed pharmacy is submitting its ordinary Drug Store Pharmacy facility license renewal application. The owner pays the fee and supplies ownership information but omits the required signed declaration concerning whether the facility complied with Massachusetts Board reporting requirements during the licensing period. No serious event has actually occurred. What must the application contain?

choices.text: An attestation of compliance with applicable 247 CMR 20 reporting requirements during the license period.
choices.why: Correct. Section 6.04(9)(c) requires this renewal attestation regardless of whether an event actually occurred.

choices.text: Only the manager's pharmacist continuing-education transcript; facility reporting compliance is never addressed on renewal.
choices.why: Incorrect. Pharmacy facility renewal attestation is separate from a pharmacist's personal CE record.

choices.text: The pharmacy must falsely claim that it submitted a serious-event report, even though none occurred.
choices.why: Incorrect. Attesting to reporting compliance is not inventing a reportable event.

choices.text: The pharmacist must file a new DEA Form 106 for each year without controlled-substance theft.
choices.why: Incorrect. Form 106 applies to qualifying theft or significant losses, not routine zero-incident renewals.

choices.text: A business license fee permanently exempts the pharmacy from all 247 CMR 20 reporting obligations.
choices.why: Incorrect. Fee payment does not substitute for the specific facility renewal attestation or reporting duties.

questions.material_novelty: Complements reporting event duties with an independent pharmacy *license-renewal attestation* of 247 CMR 20 compliance, not specific event filing or record retention.
questions.counterfactual_flip: Whether there were no reportable events or properly reported events, the attestation addresses compliance, not an event count.
questions.legal_decision: Recognize mandatory pharmacy facility renewal reporting-compliance declaration.
